text: Lesson 5 covered the catalog and software templates -- the inventory of what exists, and the way new things get created correctly. A developer portal is the layer built on top that developers actually spend their day in: one page per service, showing everything about it at once.

Open checkout-service in a Backstage-style portal and you immediately see who owns it and what it depends on, pulled straight from the catalog entity you met last lesson. Its documentation renders inline instead of living on a separate wiki tab, and its pipeline and runtime status are right there too -- no pinging three different teams in Slack just to find out if the last deploy actually passed.

That documentation piece is TechDocs, Backstage's docs-as-code system. Markdown files are committed in the same repository as the service itself, built with the static site generator MkDocs, and rendered directly inside the entity page. Because the docs live in the same pull request as the code change that makes them necessary, a reviewer can hold them to the same standard as a passing test, instead of leaving them as an unenforced chore on a wiki nobody updates.

Everything else on that page comes from Backstage's plugin model. The core application is deliberately thin -- routing, the catalog data model, authentication -- and almost everything a developer actually sees is contributed by a plugin. A CI/CD plugin shows the status of recent pipeline runs; a Kubernetes plugin shows live pod health; a cost insights plugin shows cloud spend. Each one renders as its own tab on the same entity page.

None of it works without accurate metadata underneath. A plugin reads the entity's own annotations to know what to query -- a namespace for Kubernetes, a repo slug for CI/CD -- and without that, it has nothing reliable to fetch against. The portal isn't a separate system bolted onto the catalog; it's the catalog's own data, surfaced usefully and kept current automatically.

That's the real difference from a wiki: a wiki is someone's best effort to describe a system from memory, and a portal is a live view of the system itself. Next lesson puts that live view to work -- requesting real infrastructure through the portal, backed by Terraform, with no manual ticket queue in between.
